Also, ledger_entries_rewritten adds up rewrite counts over every commit tree the SNAPSHOT appears in. A diff-only replay counts each SNAPSHOT once, so the same CollapseResult and identical ledger rewrites the plan promises will not hold.

findings.finding: Step 3 applies `diff-tree <original first-parent> <commit>` on top of 'the rewritten first parent'. In those cases the tree under `from` is not the original first parent's tree plus SNAPSHOT rewrites, so the diff lands on the wrong base and gives a wrong tree. The full-tree engine is correct here. findings.finding: The diff-based replay is defined only for a commit whose first parent was itself rewritten: it diffs `<first-parent> <commit>` and applies the result 'on top of the rewritten first parent'. In `boundary..tip`, a merged side branch can fork below the boundary, so a replayed commit's first parent (or a merge's other parent) may not be in `old_to_new` at all. The plan does not say which rewritten base such a commit builds on, which source tree the diff must be taken against so the result still equals the commit's own tree, or which mark or SHA its `from`/`merge` lines use. If it diffs against the real first parent but builds on the checkpoint, the tree silently diverges from the source, breaking the 'same old_to_new map' / identical-trees contract.

Evidence class: mid-stream SHA read-back is Unverified. `get-mark` is never named in the plan, and the repo has no fast-import marks usage (search for 'marks' in src/rebar).
findings.finding: The single fast-import stream cannot produce the rewritten SNAPSHOT blobs as described. Today's engine writes ledger `commit_sha` values that are the NEW SHAs of commits written earlier in the same rewrite. The ledger anchor uses the checkpoint SHA, and each replayed commit uses `old_to_new` entries for earlier replayed commits. In one stream those SHAs are only known inside the live fast-import process. The plan's only read-back is `--export-marks`, which is written when the stream finishes, so the stream cannot emit those SNAPSHOT contents. The plan needs a mid-stream mark read-back, such as fast-import's `get-mark :<n>` answered on stdout or `--cat-blob-fd`, with Python reading git's reply while still writing input. Otherwise the design needs a different decomposition.
scenarios: The ledger anchor's SNAPSHOT rewrite needs the checkpoint SHA, which is unknown until the stream ends.
A SNAPSHOT changed at replayed commit N references a position whose commit was replayed at N-k. Its new SHA is unavailable when N's inline data is emitted.
findings.suggested_fix: Run fast-import as a Popen with stdin and stdout pipes. After each `commit` block, write `get-mark :<n>` and read the 40-hex reply line before emitting any later commit whose SNAPSHOT rewrites need that SHA. Use that reply to grow `old_to_new` incrementally. Keep `--export-marks` only as a final cross-check. Add a red test showing that a SNAPSHOT in a replayed commit gets the new SHA of an earlier replayed commit.

findings.finding: The oracle for the equivalence test is ambiguous. findings.finding: Step 3 writes its own diff-based fast-import stream generator: one `git diff-tree -r -z --raw --no-renames <first-parent> <commit>` subprocess per replayed commit, turned into M/D lines plus `merge` lines. Stock core git already has two ways to do this that the plan never mentions or compares. First, `git fast-export --no-data --reference-excluded-parents --show-original-ids <boundary>..<tip>` writes, in one process, a stream of each commit's changes against its first parent. It includes `merge` lines, `D` deletions, blob references by original SHA (so blob contents are not copied), parents outside the range referenced by SHA, and `original-oid` lines that give the old→new mapping directly. Second, if the plan keeps its own generator, `git diff-tree --stdin` takes `<commit> <parent>` pairs in one long-lived process, the same way the plan already batches blob reads with `cat-file --batch`. At the measured scale, step 3 as written still starts about 13,119 diff-tree processes. The cost test and AC bound only `fast-import` and `cat-file`, so this per-commit process cost is never measured.
findings.location: Approach step 3 ('Replayed commits apply only their own changes'); Testing → Cost bound; AC 'The new cost test shows one `fast-import` process per collapse...'
scenarios: S3 dry run on origin/tickets: about 13,119 diff-tree spawns run alongside the single fast-import. Each one walks a 6,008-entry flat root tree. That is slower than needed, and nothing in the tests or ACs catches it.
Merge-commit handling, deletions and old→new mapping are hand-built, when `fast-export` already emits them in the stream format fast-import consumes.
findings.suggested_fix: Change Approach step 3 to list changed paths through one long-lived `git diff-tree --stdin -r -z --raw --no-renames` process, fed `<commit> <first-parent>` lines. Alternatively, explain why `git fast-export --no-data --reference-excluded-parents --show-original-ids` was not used as the stream source. Extend the cost-bound test and AC so they also check that the diff step uses a fixed number of processes, not one per replayed commit.

findings.finding: The plan relies on fast-import capabilities it has never used (mark refs in `from`/`merge`, `--export-marks`, root-tree `M 040000 <tree> ""`, and, as needed, `get-mark`), but sets no minimum git version. The probe is recorded only as 'git 2.x'. Some of these commands only exist in later git releases, so the plan should name the git version the shadow-clone run requires and either check for it or fail clearly.
